clue.text: Assault can damage present day parent

indicators.note: to damage something is to knock it out of shape, so these letters are battered into a new order

explanation.surface: A violent attack harms a mother or father on a gift-giving occasion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damage' rearranges ASSAULT and CAN together. The definition is playful: the 'parent' of the present-giving day, Christmas.
explanation.definitionFit: Father Christmas is the jolly gift-bringer figure, a kind of parent presiding over the day when presents are given.

clue.text: A cross sign is that of the alliance

parts.note: a cross drawn as a mark is the letter X
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a cross is the emblem of a political pact.
explanation.definitionFit: The Second World War pact of Germany, Italy and Japan was known as the Axis, an alliance of powers.

clue.text: Figure military displays are junk also

parts.note: tat is cheap, worthless rubbish
too means also

explanation.surface: Someone sneers that army parades are rubbish as well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'military displays' is a further sense of the answer (an Edinburgh-style army show) folded into the surface; the wordplay is TAT plus TOO.
explanation.definitionFit: A design inked permanently into the skin is a figure drawn on the body.

clue.text: Camel carrying artist is load of old toffee

indicators.note: the camel is carrying a load, so the artist's letters go inside the word camel

parts.note: RA stands for Royal Academician, a member of the Royal Academy of Arts

explanation.surface: A dromedary bearing a painter calls it all nonsense, a load of old toffee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carrying' signals the artist going inside the camel. 'A load of old toffee' is British slang for nonsense, so the surface hides the plain definition 'toffee'.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a chewy brown confection made from boiled sugar and butter, a soft kind of toffee.

clue.text: A stout porter with a round plant

indicators.note: the ale is taken with something held in it, so the round goes inside

parts.note: stout and porter are both dark kinds of ale
a round shape is the circle O

explanation.surface: A drinker orders a stout or a porter along with another round of drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' puts O inside ALE. 'round' looks like a round of drinks but simply gives the ring-shaped letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: The succulent with thick fleshy leaves, used for soothing gels, is a plant.

clue.text: Up to us, blow it, I mean hang it

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word us is read from bottom to top

parts.note: taken as written
to blow money is to spend it freely

explanation.surface: Someone exasperated says it is our decision, so forget it and string it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' turns US to SU, which is followed by SPEND. 'to', 'I mean' and the final 'it' only join the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To suspend something is to hang it from above, as with a lamp on a chain.

clue.text: Superficial art lovers playing with titled Tina

indicators.note: playing with words means messing them about, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Shallow arts dabblers are fooling around with an aristocratic woman called Tina.
explanation.walkthrough: 'playing with' rearranges TITLED and TINA together into the ten-letter answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Dabblers in the arts with no deep knowledge are amateurs whose love of art is only skin-deep.

clue.text: White pack animal may bend twitch and bolt food

parts.note: an arc is a curve or bend
a tic is an involuntary twitch
to wolf food is to gulp it down

explanation.surface: A white-coated beast may arch its back, jerk, and gulp down its dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: This pale canine of the far north hunts in groups, so it is a pack animal with a white coat.

clue.text: Rail return for romancer

indicators.note: return means the word rail comes back the other way, read right to left

explanation.surface: A railway return ticket is bought for a writer of love stories.
explanation.walkthrough: 'romancer' is used in its sense of one who invents fanciful stories, a fabricator.
explanation.definitionFit: A romancer can mean someone who tells fanciful, untrue tales, that is, a fibber.

clue.text: Mature film star's promises to be triumphant

parts.note: Victor Mature was a Hollywood star of the 1940s and 1950s
IOUs are written promises to pay

explanation.surface: An ageing actor's pledges turn out to be winners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mature' looks like an adjective (grown-up) but is the surname of the actor Victor Mature, so his first name is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has won is triumphant, having gained the victory.

clue.text: Obvious a paste book

parts.note: pâté is a savoury meat or fish paste
NT is the New Testament, a book of the Bible

explanation.surface: Someone notes that a book about spreads is plainly evident.
explanation.definitionFit: Patent as an adjective means plain or evident, as in a patent lie.

clue.text: Crown court not acceptable detaining one

indicators.note: detaining means holding someone inside, so one goes within the shortened word
not means the acceptable letter is left out of the word court

parts.note: U means upper-class and so socially acceptable, as in U and non-U
taken as written

explanation.surface: A royal court finds it unacceptable to hold someone in custody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes U, leaving CORT, and 'detaining' signals the insertion. U for 'acceptable' comes from the British U (upper-class) versus non-U distinction.
explanation.definitionFit: A coronet is a small crown worn by nobles below the monarch.

clue.text: Wicked light supporters

parts.note: wicked here means having wicks, so the clue describes branched stands holding several wick-bearing lights, not evil backers

explanation.surface: Evil people who back someone only lightly.
explanation.definitionFit: These are ornamental branched holders that carry several candles, each candle being a lit wick.

clue.text: Discerning incorrectly that it means revoking

indicators.note: written incorrectly means the letters are out of their proper order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Getting one's judgement wrong amounts to cancelling something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'incorrectly' rearranges DISCERNING; 'that it means' merely links.
explanation.definitionFit: Rescinding a law or order is cancelling it officially, i.e. revoking it.

clue.text: Implied I was beset by discretion

indicators.note: beset by means surrounded on all sides, so I sits within the word for discretion

parts.note: tact is discretion in dealing with others

explanation.surface: Someone recalls being hemmed in by everyone's careful silence on the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'was beset by' puts I inside TACT.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacit means understood without being stated, so it is implied rather than spoken.

clue.text: Knowing how to get costing wrong?

indicators.note: getting a word wrong suggests its letters are muddled, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks how to make a mess of a budget estimate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' rearranges COSTING; 'how to get' joins definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnostic means relating to knowledge, especially esoteric spiritual knowledge.

clue.text: Earn the title obese vulgar and loutish

definitions.meaning: to earn a sum before deductions is to take it in total, before tax

explanation.surface: A fat person is branded crude and boorish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the title obese' points to a third sense, very fat, alongside the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to make as total income before tax; as an adjective it means coarse and crude.

clue.text: One gathers a lot of fat as landowner

indicators.note: gathers signals one piece being drawn inside another, here the one going into the fat

parts.note: lard is a mass of pig fat
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A man piles on a great deal of weight in his role as an estate owner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gathers' places I inside LARD. The answer is a Scottish word: the owner of a large estate.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland a laird is the proprietor of an estate, a landed proprietor.

clue.text: No order for quiet nourishment

parts.note: taken as written
sh is the command telling someone to be silent

explanation.surface: No instruction is given to keep silent about food.
explanation.walkthrough: NOSH is British slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosh is informal British slang for food, which is what provides nourishment.

clue.text: Keen on taking in a pint of ale

indicators.note: taking in means containing, so the answer is concealed within the words a pint of

explanation.surface: Someone fond of drinking downs a pint of beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking in' signals a run of letters within 'a pINT Of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Into, in informal use, means enthusiastic about something, as in being into jazz.

clue.text: Centre of the haze lies Germany

indicators.note: something that lies in the haze sits within it, so Germany's letter goes inside the mist

parts.note: mist is a light haze
D is the international vehicle code for Germany

explanation.surface: Germany is shrouded in fog at the heart of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lies' puts D inside MIST; 'of the' links definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: The midst of something is its middle, the heart or core of it.

clue.text: Spots a little rouble in trouble

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'Spots a little rouble in trouble', gives no parse for MEASLES: no reading of 'a little rouble in trouble' builds the letters, and a search of the exact text finds no other version.
annotationWithheld.clue: Spots a little rouble in trouble

clue.text: Mothers broken the flask

indicators.note: broken means smashed apart, so the letters of mothers are reassembled differently

explanation.surface: Mothers have smashed the vacuum bottle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broken' rearranges MOTHERS; 'the' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A Thermos is a trademark vacuum flask that keeps drinks hot or cold.

clue.text: Expletive at east enders holding pit man

indicators.note: holding means keeping inside, so the outer letters wrap around the mine and the man
the enders of a word are its first and last letters, here taken from east

parts.note: taken as written
he is the pronoun for a man

explanation.surface: An oath is sworn at Londoners from the East End who are holding a miner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enders' gives E and T, the first and last letters of 'east'; 'holding' signals the wrap. 'East Enders' looks like Londoners from the East End (and the TV soap EastEnders), but it is a letter-picking device.
explanation.definitionFit: An epithet can be an abusive word or term, much like a curse or swear word.

clue.text: Star supporter in westerns

parts.note: star here is the badge pinned on a lawman's chest, so the clue describes the cowboy-film figure who wears it rather than a supporting actor

explanation.surface: An actor playing second fiddle to the lead in cowboy films.
explanation.definitionFit: In cowboy films the county lawman wears a star-shaped badge on his shirt, so he literally supports a star.

clue.text: Bucolic game will stick to no ending

parts.note: RU is rugby union, a ball game

indicators.note: no ending means the word stick loses its final letter

explanation.surface: A country pastime will be stuck to without end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no ending' removes K from STICK to leave STIC; 'will' and 'to' only link.
explanation.definitionFit: Bucolic means relating to the countryside, which is what rustic also means.

clue.text: No little start runs after snakes

indicators.note: no here means without, so the first letter of little is taken out of the runs

parts.note: runs in tights or stockings are called ladders in Britain

indicators.note: start points to the first letter of little

explanation.surface: No small beginning: the race runs after the serpents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'start' gives L from 'little'; 'No' removes it from LADDERS. A ladder is the British word for a run in tights.
explanation.definitionFit: Adders are venomous vipers, the only poisonous snakes native to Britain.

clue.text: Top one in a million

indicators.note: in places the million inside the word for one

parts.note: an ace counts as one in cards and on dice
M is the abbreviation for a million

explanation.surface: Someone is the best, a one-in-a-million talent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts M inside ACE. The surface reads as the idiom 'one in a million'.
explanation.definitionFit: The acme is the highest point or peak, the very summit of something.

clue.text: Foretell a person with energy

parts.note: bod is British slang for a person
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: A fortune-teller predicts a lively individual.
explanation.walkthrough: BOD is informal British slang for a person or body.
explanation.definitionFit: To bode is to be an omen of something, as in 'it bodes ill', so it means to portend.

clue.text: Mad reason for movement

parts.note: loco is slang for crazy
a motion is a proposal put forward as a reasoned case in debate

explanation.surface: A crazy argument is advanced for a political campaign.
explanation.definitionFit: Locomotion is the act or power of moving from place to place.

clue.text: A game book ended in the litter

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held, 'A game book ended in the litter', gives RU + NT for the letters but no contiguous words define the answer ('ended in the litter' cannot stand for the smallest animal), and a search of the exact text finds no other version.
annotationWithheld.clue: A game book ended in the litter

clue.text: Wise man and fool is material

parts.note: a seer is a prophet or sage
a sucker is a gullible person, someone easily fooled

explanation.surface: A sage and a simpleton are the stuff of the matter.
explanation.definitionFit: Seersucker is a puckered cotton or linen fabric, a cloth used for summer suits.
